# Exact double-knot reduction for the diagonal envelope deficit

This note proves a finite-parameter variational reduction. It does not
prove the proposed sharp global deficit bound. In particular, it retains
the boundary where the radius slope tends to zero.

Fix d>=2, t=1/(d+1), Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d. For 0<a<=1 and
0<=beta<=at put r_h=(1-ah)_+, q_h=t-beta h, p_h=t+beta(h+1).
On the positive-radius indices, both thresholds are >=t r_h. Define
the diagonal lower envelope

    E(q,r)=d^d q^(d-1)(r-dq)_+       (r>0,q>0),

and set its value to zero for r=0. Define the exact envelope deficit

    D(a,beta)=Gamma sum_(h>=0) r_h^d
              -sum_(h>=0)[E(q_h,r_h)+E(p_h,r_h)].        (1)

Only finitely many terms are nonzero for a>0. At positive radius,
q_h>=t r_h>0 throughout this parameter domain. Thus no undefined
negative-threshold expression enters (1).

## 1. Precise compact-domain conclusion

For every 0<epsilon<=1, the maximum of D on

    epsilon<=a<=1,       0<=beta<=at                     (2)

is attained. Its value is no greater than the maximum of zero,
the maximum on the edge a=epsilon, and its values at the admissible
double knots

    beta=t(H-J)/[d H(2J+1)],
    a=t(H+J+1)/[H(2J+1)],                               (3)

where H>=1 and J>=0 are integers satisfying

    J<=H,       H<=(2d+1)J+d,

and (3) lies in (2). There are only finitely many relevant knots in
each fixed domain (2). Boundary coincidences are included.

The a=epsilon edge is NOT discarded. Consequently this theorem makes
no unproved assertion about a,beta tending to zero or about the
attainment of an unrestricted maximum on a>0.

## 2. First reduction at fixed beta

On (2), only indices h<=1/epsilon need be retained. All terms are
continuous, including at zero radii, so D is continuous on the compact
domain and its maximum exists.

Fix beta. On every interval of a between envelope activation knots,
each active envelope term is affine in a: its positive threshold is
fixed and its remaining factor is affine. The mass term
Gamma sum_h(1-ah)_+^d is convex. Hence D is convex on each such
interval. Mass-zero knots do not spoil this assertion, since the
positive-part dth power is convex across them.

The only envelope activation knots depending on a are

    a=d beta+t/H                 (left knot, H>=1),     (4)
    a=t/H-d beta(1+1/H)          (right knot, H>=1).    (5)

The right cap at h=0 has its separate activation at beta=t/d.
At fixed beta it is independent of a.

A convex function on an interval is bounded above by the larger of
its endpoint values. Therefore a maximizer can be moved to an edge
of (2) or to a knot (4) or (5), without decreasing D. No derivative
of a selected maximizer is used.

## 3. Convexity along a left knot

Fix H>=1 and follow a=d beta+t/H within (2). The hard-tilt condition
beta<=at is exactly beta<=t/H. Left-active indices are j<H, and for
such an index write

    q=t-beta j,
    ell=t(1-j/H),
    r=dq+ell,
    x=ell/q in [0,1].

The upper bound x<=1 follows from beta<=t/H. For j>0 the second
derivative of Gamma*r^d-E(q,r), after dividing by the positive
factor d^d(d-1)j^2 q^(d-2), is

    Gamma*d*(1+x/d)^(d-2)-(d-2)x.                        (6)

This is positive on [0,1]. For x>0, the ratio
(1+x/d)^(d-2)/x is decreasing: its logarithmic derivative has
numerator (d-3)x-d<0 on that interval. It therefore suffices to
check x=1. There the difference in (6) is exactly

    d^3/(d+1)^2-(d-2)=(3d+2)/(d+1)^2>0.

At x=0 positivity is immediate. At j=0 the left contribution and its
mass are constant. Indices with no active left envelope contribute
only a convex mass term.

For a right-active index j along the same knot, put

    p=t+beta(j+1),
    ell_R=t(1-j/H)-d beta(2j+1).

The second derivative of its right envelope is

    d^d(d-1)(j+1)p^(d-3)
       *[(d-2)(j+1)ell_R-2d(2j+1)p].                   (7)

Within the hard-tilt domain, an active envelope has ell_R<=p.
The bracket in (7) is therefore strictly negative. Thus each active
right envelope is concave along the left knot. Subtracting it
preserves the convexity already proved for mass minus left envelope.

It follows that D is convex on every segment of this left knot between
right-envelope activations, including the own right activation at
beta=t/d. At an activation the derivative can jump in the other
direction; the proof therefore keeps that point as an endpoint,
rather than claiming global convexity along the knot.

## 4. Convexity along a right knot

Fix H>=1 and follow a=t/H-d beta(1+1/H) within (2). For a right-active
index j<H, write p=t+beta(j+1) and r=dp+ell. The hard-tilt condition
implies x=ell/p in [0,1]. The derivative ratio is

    eta=r'/p'=d j(1+1/H)/(j+1) in [0,d].

The second derivative of Gamma*r^d-E(p,r), divided by the positive
factor d^d(d-1)p^(d-2)(p')^2, equals

    A eta^2-2eta+d^2-(d-2)(d+x),
    A=d(d+x)^(d-2)/(d+1)^d.                             (8)

Because A*d<=d^2/(d+1)^2<1, (8) decreases in eta on [0,d]. At eta=d
it is precisely the positive expression (6). Thus mass minus its
right envelope is convex along the knot. This also handles j=0,
where eta=0. Indices with no right envelope contribute convex mass.

For a left-active index j along this right knot,

    q=t-beta j,
    ell_L=t(1-j/H)+d beta j(2+1/H).

Its second derivative is

    d^d(d-1)j^2 q^(d-3)
       *[(d-2)ell_L-2d(2+1/H)q].                       (9)

The active hard-tilt regime gives ell_L<=q. The bracket in (9) is
negative for j>0, and j=0 is constant. Hence the left envelope is
concave on each active segment. Combining with (8) proves convexity
of D along the right knot between left activations.

All powers in (6)--(9) are evaluated at positive thresholds on active
pieces. The appearances of q^(d-3) or p^(d-3) at d=2 therefore cause
no singular endpoint assumption. Limits at a supporting knot are
handled by continuity of (1).

## 5. Intersections and harmless outer edges

The previous two sections move a maximum on either type of knot to
a domain endpoint or an intersection of a left and a right activation.
Solving the left equation for index H and right equation for index
J>=1 gives exactly (3). Taking J=0 denotes the own-right activation
beta=t/d and gives the same formula. Nonnegative beta requires J<=H;
the hard-tilt inequality beta<=at simplifies exactly to
H<=(2d+1)J+d.

On beta=at, every left envelope equals Gamma*r_h^d, so D<=0.
On a=1, only the central radius contributes positive mass, and its
left envelope is already Gamma; again D<=0.

On beta=0, put

    S_p(c)=sum_(h>=0)(1-ch)_+^p.

Then the total envelope is 2Gamma*S_1((d+1)a), while the mass target
is Gamma*S_d(a). The decreasing-function Riemann bound gives

    S_d(a)<=1+1/[(d+1)a].

The exact convex trapezoid inequality for the nonnegative linear
truncation gives

    2S_1((d+1)a)>=1+1/[(d+1)a].

Thus D<=0 on this edge as well. These estimates are valid for every
a>0, including when a sampling endpoint hits zero.

The remaining boundary is a=epsilon, which the theorem explicitly
retains. This completes the compact-domain double-knot reduction.

## 6. What is still not proved

The proposed universal bound is

    D(a,beta)<=Gamma sum_(h>=1)(1-2h/(d+1))_+^d.

The right side is attained at H=1,J=0. The reduction above does not
compare all other integer pairs H,J with that pair. Nor does it
bound uniformly the retained a=epsilon edge as epsilon tends to zero.
Those are genuine remaining steps. No numerical search result supplies
either step.
